pages.title: DNA, in plain words
text: Every living cell carries a set of instructions written in DNA: a long molecule shaped like a rope ladder with a twist in it.
The rungs come in four letters, A, T, C and G. A always pairs with T, and C with G, so either half of the ladder can rebuild the other.
That pairing is how a cell copies itself, and how a parent hands a copy on.
A human cell holds about three billion letter pairs. Read out at one a second, that would take you nearly a century.
pages.story: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray picture Photo 51, taken at King's College London in 1952, helped Francis Crick and James Watson work out the double helix in Cambridge in 1953.

pages.title: Genes and alleles
text: A gene is a stretch of DNA that does one job, often the recipe for one protein, such as a pigment.
Most animals carry two copies of each gene, one from each parent. The different versions a gene comes in are its alleles.
The makings in your Stud Book are alleles: the plain coat and the coloured coat are two versions of one gene.
Humans have roughly 20,000 genes that make proteins, far fewer than scientists expected before they counted.
pages.story: The Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen coined the word gene in 1909. William Bateson's longer word, allelomorph, got shortened to allele.

pages.title: New mutations
pages.hint: Hatch a sport, or ask Dr Keir what one is.
text: A mutation is a change in the DNA letters: a copying slip, or damage from sunlight or chemicals.
Every person is born with a few dozen new ones that neither parent had. Nearly all of them do nothing at all.
A few change a protein, and a very few change something you can see, such as a coat.
Mutation is random. It doesn't aim at anything useful. Selection is what keeps the useful ones.
pages.story: In the game about one hatchling in sixty-four is a sport, so you see them. Mutations that show are far rarer in real animals, which is why breeders noticed and named every one.

pages.title: Inbreeding and pedigrees
pages.hint: Be refused a close pairing, or ask Dr Keir about close kin.
text: Most harmful alleles are recessive and rare. Everyone carries a few, and they do no harm while the other copy works.
Relatives share alleles. Breed close kin and their young get two copies of the same rare fault far more often. That's inbreeding depression.
So conservation breeders keep a studbook: who is whose parent, back through the generations, to pair animals as unrelated as possible.

Rare breeds, zoo programmes and the Scottish wildcat all work this way. The wildcat breeders also test for domestic cat genes, because hybrids are the bigger threat. Saving Wildcats began releasing cats in the Cairngorms in 2023.
pages.story: Every Przewalski's horse alive today descends from about a dozen caught in the wild around 1900, and a studbook tracks every birth to keep them as varied as they can be.

pages.title: Hybrid vigour and the mule
pages.hint: Meet a hybrid, or a sterile pairing, at the farm.
text: Cross two unrelated lines and the young are often hardier than either parent. Breeders call it hybrid vigour; biologists call it heterosis.
Partly it's inbreeding run backwards: with two different copies, a rare fault on one side is covered by the other.
Cross two species and the young may be sterile. A mule has 63 chromosomes, and they can't all pair up to make eggs or sperm.
Hybrid names put the father first: a liger has a lion for a father and a tiger for a mother.
pages.story: People have bred mules for thousands of years, for strength and stamina, knowing full well there would be no second generation.

pages.title: Natural selection
pages.hint: Watch the moor model for a few seasons.
text: Some creatures survive and breed better than others because of what they inherited, so their alleles become commoner.
Nobody chooses. A kestrel just eats the ones it can see.
It needs three things: variety, inheritance, and some of the variety mattering.
Selection only works with what is there. It can't invent a colour; mutation does that.
pages.story: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the idea separately. Their papers were read together at the Linnean Society in London on 1 July 1858, and On the Origin of Species came out the next year.

pages.title: The peppered moth
text: The peppered moth rests on tree bark by day. The usual pale, speckled form vanishes against lichen.
In the 1800s soot from the mills blackened the trees round Manchester. A dark form, first recorded there in 1848, became the commonest one.
After the Clean Air Act of 1956 the air cleared, the lichen came back, and so did the pale moths.
Birds did the choosing. Bernard Kettlewell's experiments in the 1950s, and Michael Majerus's later ones, showed birds take the moths that stand out.
pages.story: In 2016 scientists traced the dark form to a single change in one gene, called cortex.

pages.title: Dolly, 1996
text: Dolly the sheep was born at the Roslin Institute on 5 July 1996, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.
Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell's team took the nucleus of a cell from a ewe's udder and put it into an egg cell whose own nucleus had been taken out.
It proved that an adult cell still holds the instructions for a whole animal.
Cloning copies; breeding shuffles. Dolly had no new combination in her at all.
pages.story: Dolly lived until 2003 and is on display at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh.

pages.title: The Human Genome Project
pages.hint: Ask Dr Keir what has happened since Dolly.
text: Between 1990 and 2003 labs around the world read the letters of a human genome, all three billion or so.
The Wellcome Sanger Institute near Cambridge read nearly a third of it.
It took thirteen years. Today a whole genome can be read in a day or two for a few hundred pounds.
England's 100,000 Genomes Project, finished in 2018, read the genomes of NHS patients with rare diseases and cancer.
pages.story: The project was declared complete in April 2003, fifty years almost to the month after the double helix paper.

pages.title: CRISPR: editing genes
pages.hint: Ask Dr Keir what has happened since Dolly.
text: CRISPR is a trick borrowed from bacteria, which use it to chop up the DNA of viruses that attack them.
Scientists can aim it at one spot in a genome, cut there, and let the cell mend the cut, sometimes with a new piece put in.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for turning it into a tool.
In November 2023 the UK became the first country to approve a CRISPR treatment, Casgevy, for sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia.
pages.story: Researchers at the Roslin Institute have used gene editing to make pigs that resist PRRS, a costly virus of pigs.

pages.title: Gene banks
pages.hint: Ask Dr Keir about seed banks.
text: A gene bank keeps living variety safe against the day it is needed: seeds, frozen cells, sperm and embryos.
Kew's Millennium Seed Bank at Wakehurst, in West Sussex, opened in 2000. It holds seeds of tens of thousands of wild plant species, dried and frozen.
Dry, cold seeds can last for decades, and some for centuries.
Rare breed keepers freeze semen and embryos for the same reason, so a breed's variety can outlive its last animals.
pages.story: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, dug into an Arctic mountainside in Norway and opened in 2008, keeps spare copies of crop seeds from gene banks all over the world.

challenges.title: Medium marks
challenges.ask: Dr Keir's challenge: what's the chance this one hatches with medium markings?
challenges.brief: Pair any two at a farm, and tell me the chance of medium markings. Bold and faint make medium, remember, so nothing's hidden.

challenges.title: Daughter or son
challenges.ask: Dr Keir's challenge: what's the chance this one is a daughter?
challenges.brief: Next pairing, tell me the chance of a daughter. Then ask yourself which parent decided it. In beasts it's the father; in birds it's the mother.

challenges.title: A coloured coat
challenges.ask: Dr Keir's challenge: what's the chance of a coloured coat? Mind what a plain parent might be hiding.
challenges.brief: Tell me the chance of a coloured coat. If a plain parent hasn't been tested, it might be carrying, so the honest answer can be a range.

challenges.title: Tortoiseshell
challenges.ask: Dr Keir's challenge: what's the chance this one is tortoiseshell?
challenges.brief: Tortoiseshell. Ginger rides on the sex chromosome, so work out who can be tortie at all before you work out the odds.

challenges.title: Frame
challenges.ask: Dr Keir's challenge: on average, how many Frame pluses would young of these two have?
challenges.brief: Frame's four genes adding up. Tell me how big their young would be on average. Galton would want you to think about the middle.
